title: Lesson 3: The Notes on the Fretboard
intro: Knowing where the notes are turns shapes into music you understand. You do not need to memorise the whole neck at once: learn strings 6 and 5 first (they hold the roots of almost every chord), then use octave shapes to find the rest.

items: Name any note on strings 6 and 5 up to fret 12.
Find the same note an octave higher with an octave shape.
Find the same pitch in several places.
A tuned guitar. Know the musical alphabet A B C D E F G, and that there is no sharp between E and F or between B and C (see Notation (#/arts/music-theory/sound-and-pitch/notation)).

blocks.alt: A guitar neck drawn horizontally with the high e string on top and frets 0 to 12. Every natural note is a labelled blue dot (C in red) and the sharps are small grey labels; fret 12 repeats the open-string names.
blocks.caption: Every note in the first 12 frets. Natural notes are labelled; the C's are red so you can see how one note repeats across the neck.

items: Step 1. Play the open low E string and say 'E'. Each fret raises it by one semitone.
Step 2. Play fret 1 and say 'F' (E to F has no sharp between them). Fret 2: F♯. Fret 3: G. Fret 4: G♯. Fret 5: A.
Step 3. Continue: fret 6 A♯, fret 7 B, fret 8 C (B to C has no sharp), fret 9 C♯, fret 10 D, fret 11 D♯, fret 12 E again (the double dot), an octave above the open string.
Step 4. Now play only the natural notes and say each name: open E, 1 F, 3 G, 5 A, 7 B, 8 C, 10 D, 12 E. Use Step ▶ below to check yourself.
Step 5. Landmarks to remember: G at 3, A at 5, C at 8, D at 10.

widget.title: Natural notes on string 6, then string 5

examples.label: String 6: E F G A B C D E
String 5: A B C D E F G A

items: Step 1. String 5 starts on A. Natural notes: open A, fret 2 B, 3 C, 5 D, 7 E, 8 F, 10 G, 12 A.
Step 2. Landmarks: C at 3, D at 5, E at 7, G at 10.
Step 3. Quiz yourself: pick a random fret on string 6 or 5, name the note, then check with the diagram.
Step 1. Play A on string 6 fret 5. Now go two strings up (string 4) and two frets higher (fret 7): another A, one octave higher. This is the octave shape from strings 6 and 5.
Step 2. From string 4 or 3, the shape is two strings up and three frets higher, because the jump crosses the G–B gap: G on string 4 fret 5 → G on string 2 fret 8.
Step 3. String 6 and string 1 at the same fret are two octaves apart: play both at fret 5 (two A's).
Step 4. With these shapes, any note you know on strings 6 or 5 gives you the same note on strings 4, 3, 2 and 1.

examples.label: A: string 6 fret 5 → string 4 fret 7 → string 1 fret 5

items: Step 1. Play the open A string (A2). The same pitch is on string 6 at fret 5. Play both: identical. Going down a string (thicker) you go 5 frets up for the same pitch (4 frets when going from the B string to the G string).

Step 2. Middle C (C4) is on string 2 fret 1, string 3 fret 5, string 4 fret 10, string 5 fret 15 and string 6 fret 20. Choosing where to play a note is part of playing guitar: it changes the tone and how easily the next note falls under your fingers.

widget.title: Where are C4 and E4? (all places light up)

items: 3 min: say the natural notes on string 6 up and down, then on string 5.
3 min: random fret quiz on strings 6 and 5 (close your eyes, pick a fret, name it, check).
4 min: for each natural note on string 6, play its octave on string 4.
2 min: find all the E's on the neck up to fret 12 (there are 8 places, counting the two open E strings).

blocks.title: Find it
blocks.text: Where are the two lowest D pitches on the neck in standard tuning?
solution: The lowest note is E2, so there is no D2. The lowest D is D3: open string 4, string 5 fret 5 and string 6 fret 10.
The next is D4: string 2 fret 3, string 3 fret 7, string 4 fret 12 and string 5 fret 17.

blocks.title: Octave
blocks.text: Your root is B♭ on string 5 fret 1. Where is the B♭ an octave up?
solution: From string 5: two strings up (string 3), two frets higher: string 3 fret 3.

blocks.text: Sources: Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press.
